verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul turns to Abraham — the father of the Jewish people and the paradigm of covenant relationship with God — to demonstrate that justification by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the original pattern. If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have grounds for boasting before other men. But the critical phrase is 'before God': no human achievement, no matter how impressive, constitutes grounds for boasting before the Holy One of Israel. The courtroom that matters is not the court of human opinion.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary: Genesis 15:6 is Paul's proof text, and its logic is decisive: Abraham's righteousness was 'counted' (elogisthē — imputed, reckoned, credited) to him, not earned. The bookkeeping metaphor is precise: wages are not a gift, they are a debt owed to a worker. But Abraham was not working; he was believing. God was not paying a debt; he was giving a gift. The structure of justification is grace from beginning to end: the righteousness credited is not Abraham's own; it is the verdict of a gracious God upon a trusting man.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Justifies the ungodly' — this phrase was scandalous in Paul's Jewish context, for the law explicitly condemned the justification of the wicked (Proverbs 17:15; Exodus 23:7). Yet this is exactly what God does in the gospel: he declares righteous those who are, in themselves, ungodly. This is the 'wonderful exchange' (Calvin): Christ takes our ungodliness; we receive his righteousness. The one who does not work — who has abandoned all trust in personal performance — and simply believes: this person receives the verdict 'righteous' as a free gift from the God who alone can give it.

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary: David's beatitude from Psalm 32 confirms the Abrahamic pattern: the blessed man is not the man who has no lawless deeds but the man whose lawless deeds are forgiven. The blessing is not the absence of sin but the removal of its condemnation. 'Covered' is the Old Testament word for atonement (kāpar): the sin is not ignored or minimized but covered — placed under the blood of sacrifice, hidden from the eyes of the righteous Judge. The gospel does not pretend sin away; it deals with it at the cost of the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive and negative of the same magnificent reality: the Lord 'will not count' (ou mē logisētai) the sin of the forgiven person. The same verb used of imputing righteousness (v. 3) is here used of not imputing sin. Double imputation: our sin is counted to Christ; Christ's righteousness is counted to us. David wrote this after the darkest chapter of his life — adultery, murder, deception — and this is the psalm that resulted. The man who knew his sin most deeply also knew most deeply the grace that does not count it.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he had been circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul presses the chronological question with rabbinic precision. Genesis 15 (Abraham's faith counted as righteousness) precedes Genesis 17 (circumcision) by at least fourteen years. This is not a trivial point — it means Abraham was justified as an uncircumcised man, as a Gentile. His justification is therefore the paradigm for Gentile justification, not a special case reserved for the covenant people. The sign came after the reality; the reality was already present by faith alone.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary: Circumcision was a seal of a righteousness already possessed by faith — a sign that pointed to and confirmed an existing reality. Abraham is therefore the father of two groups: the uncircumcised who believe (the Gentile church) and the circumcised who walk in the footsteps of his faith (believing Israel). Both inherit through faith, not through the sign. The sign matters — it is a God-given seal — but it seals what faith has already received, not what works have earned.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now extends his argument to the promise God made to Abraham — that he would be heir of the world, that his offspring would be numberless, that through him all nations would be blessed. This promise, Paul insists, was given through the righteousness of faith, not through the law. The law cannot be the means of inheriting the promise, because the law can only pronounce wrath (it condemns those who fail to keep it); if the promise depends on law-keeping, the promise is void for everyone.

The portrait of Abraham's faith in vv. 17–21 is one of the most moving passages in the entire New Testament. Abraham — "as good as dead" at a hundred years old, Sarah's womb "dead" — hoped against hope. He did not weaken in faith when he considered the hopeless biological reality. He did not waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that what God had promised He was also able to perform. This is faith in its purest form: not faith in the circumstances, not faith in human possibility, but faith in the God who raises the dead and calls into existence things that do not exist (v. 17).

And then the connection to us: this was written not for Abraham's sake alone but for ours — for those who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. The resurrection is not merely the proof that Jesus is who He claimed to be; it is the declaration that the justification He accomplished has been accepted. The empty tomb is God's receipt for a debt paid in full.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of His deity but the declaration that His atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in His death; it is faith in the God who raised Him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond Him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is emptied and the promise is nullified,
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise to Abraham (Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22) was cosmic in scope: 'heir of the world.' Paul reads the Abrahamic blessing in its full New Testament dimensions: the inheritance is not merely Canaan but the renewed creation, the world made new. And this promise came through faith, not through law-keeping — because the law did not yet exist. If the inheritance depended on law-observance, faith would be drained of its meaning and the promise made conditional on human performance — which is precisely what the promise was designed to transcend.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary: Law and promise operate on different principles. Law requires performance; failure triggers judgment. Promise requires trust; reception is by grace. If the inheritance came by law, it would be uncertain — permanently at risk of disqualification by the next failure. Because it comes by promise through faith, it is guaranteed (bebaian — secure, firm, legally certain). Grace makes the promise certain precisely because grace does not depend on the fluctuating performance of the beneficiary.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham's faith is defined by its object: the God who raises the dead and calls things into existence from nothing. This is creation-faith and resurrection-faith — trusting the God for whom impossibility is simply the normal starting point of his greatest works. 'In hope he believed against hope' — there was no natural basis for hope; every human indicator pointed to hopelessness. But Abraham's hope was not natural; it was theological: he knew who God was. Keller: 'Faith is not optimism about circumstances; it is confidence in the character of God.'

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham 'considered' his circumstances — he was not naive about them. He looked at his body, recognized its deadness, looked at Sarah's womb, recognized its barrenness — and still did not waver. This is mature faith: not the refusal to face facts, but the refusal to allow facts to have the final word. The final word belongs to the one who spoke the promise. And as Abraham gave glory to God — as he credited God with the ability to do what he had said — his own faith was strengthened. Worship and faith reinforce each other.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary: The simplest possible description of saving faith: fully convinced that God is able to do what he has promised. Not convinced by the evidence, not persuaded by circumstances, but convinced of God's ability and God's faithfulness. This is the faith that Paul has been arguing justifies — not intellectual assent to propositions, not emotional experience, but the settled confidence of a soul resting its entire weight on the reliability of the God who speaks and keeps his word.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith 'was counted to him as righteousness.' But the words 'it was counted to him' were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–23
verseByVerse.commentary:
The connection between Abraham's justification and ours is explicit: the Genesis text was not written merely as biography. It was written as theology — specifically, as the pattern for how God justifies all who believe. The same verb (logizomai — to count, reckon, credit) that was used of Abraham's faith being credited as righteousness is the verb used of our faith being credited. The pattern is identical because the God is identical and the mechanism is identical.

This is Paul's hermeneutical principle for reading the Old Testament: narrative is theological, history is instructive, biography is paradigmatic. The story of Abraham is not merely a chapter in the history of Israel; it is the template for understanding how any human being — in any age, of any ethnicity — stands righteous before God. By faith. Through grace. Credited, not earned. The same yesterday, today, and forever.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallelism of v. 25 is exquisite: delivered up for our trespasses — raised for our justification. Death dealt with sin; resurrection accomplished justification. The cross is where our guilt was carried; the empty tomb is where our acquittal was declared. This means that the Christian's confidence in their justification rests not merely on the death of Christ (sufficient) but on the resurrection of Christ (declared). A dead Saviour might have died for our sins, but could not justify us; a risen Saviour has been declared by God to have accomplished what He came to accomplish.

"Raised for our justification" — the resurrection is not merely apologetic (proving Jesus is Lord) but forensic (declaring the sinner righteous). When God raised Jesus from the dead, He was saying: the price has been paid; the sin has been dealt with; the one who trusts in this risen Lord is acquitted. The empty tomb is the receipt for every sin of every believer — paid, cancelled, gone.

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Romans 5 is the hinge of the letter. Behind us lie three chapters of diagnosis and one chapter of remedy; ahead lie three chapters of Christian experience and life. Chapter 5 stands at the turning point, summarising the achievements of justification (vv. 1–11) before setting those achievements within the grandest possible framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose actions determined the destiny of all humanity (vv. 12–21).

The opening "therefore" connects everything that follows to everything Paul has argued. Because we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God. We have access to grace. We stand in hope. We can even boast in our sufferings. And the love of God — poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit — is the guarantee that the hope will not put us to shame. The person justified by faith does not merely have a changed legal status; she has entered a new world, a new relationship, a new story whose ending is already written.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Peace, Access, Hope, and the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." This sentence is the great sigh of relief at the centre of the letter. Three chapters of accumulated guilt — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the universal verdict of Scripture, the silencing of every mouth — and now: peace. Not merely the absence of war, but the shalom of a relationship fully restored. The hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature has been dealt with at the cross, and the one who has received the verdict of justification stands in the peace of a fully settled relationship with God.

Paul adds to peace the gift of access (v. 2) — "through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." Access was a technical term for the privilege of being brought into the presence of a king. The justified sinner has not merely been acquitted; she has been given permanent, unimpeded access to the throne of God. She does not approach on the basis of her spiritual performance on any given day; she stands in grace — a position of favour that does not fluctuate with her feelings or her faithfulness.

The boasting in sufferings (vv. 3–5) is one of the most counter-intuitive things Paul writes. He does not merely say we can endure suffering; he says we rejoice in it — because suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame because the love of God has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit. The chain is unbreakable. And the certainty of hope rests not on our own resilience but on the Spirit-given experience of being loved by God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peace with God and the Assurance of Faith

Romans 5:1 is a foundation stone of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The believer has peace with God — not the peace she feels on spiritually good days, but the objective peace established by the accomplished work of Christ received by faith. The Reformation recovered this against the Roman Catholic teaching that assurance is presumption: on the contrary, to doubt one's justification when God has spoken the verdict is to call God's word into question. As Calvin wrote, faith without assurance is not the faith of the New Testament. The peace of Romans 5:1 is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the finished work of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first-century world had no shortage of philosophical frameworks for enduring suffering — Stoic resignation, Epicurean avoidance, Platonic transcendence. None of them grounded suffering in the love of a personal God or gave it redemptive purpose. Paul's rejoicing in suffering (vv. 3–5) was genuinely new: suffering has a trajectory, and that trajectory ends in hope that is guaranteed by the Spirit. Now: In an age that treats suffering as the enemy of the good life, to be medicated, minimised, or avoided at all costs, Romans 5:3–5 offers a radically different framework. Suffering is not the enemy of Christian hope; it is one of its primary instruments. The Christian who suffers well — who endures, who builds character, who hopes — is not an anomaly but a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace with God is not the same as peace about God. It is not subjective tranquillity or the absence of spiritual anxiety; it is the objective end of hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature. The war is over. Christ made peace by the blood of His cross (Colossians 1:20). The person who has been justified has crossed from a state of divine enmity (v. 10 — "while we were enemies") to a state of peace. This is not metaphor; it is forensic reality.

The escalation from peace (v. 1) to standing in grace (v. 2) to hope of glory (v. 2) is deliberate. Justification does not merely settle the past; it opens the future. The one who stands in grace has a trajectory — the glory of God, the full conformity to Christ, the resurrection body, the new creation. The present standing and the future destination are both secured by the same grace received by the same faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul has just spoken of rejoicing in the hope of the glory of God (v. 2); now he speaks of rejoicing in sufferings — and the conjunction 'not only that' suggests the second is as natural as the first. Suffering is not merely to be endured; it is to be the occasion of joy, because it is the workshop in which endurance (hypomonē — steadfast remaining under pressure) is forged. Endurance produces tested character (dokimē — the quality that has passed the assay); character produces hope. The process is not automatic but requires the presence of the Spirit described in v. 5.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary: This hope does not disappoint or shame — it is not wishful thinking that will be exposed as fantasy. Its guarantee is the Holy Spirit, who has been poured out into the believer's heart as the firstfruits of the coming glory. The love of God is not merely an objective fact about God's attitude; it has been experientially poured into (not trickled into, but flooded into) the believer's inner life. Ferguson notes that this internal witness of the Spirit to the love of God is what sustains the rejoicing of vv. 3–4 through the darkest seasons of suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary: 'At the right time' (kata kairon) — the crucifixion was not an accident of history but an event scheduled in the eternal purpose of God, falling at the precise moment of human helplessness. 'Weak' — not morally neutral but spiritually incapacitated, unable to help ourselves. For the ungodly — not for those who had earned divine favor, but for those who were in active opposition to God. The contrast with human heroism (one might conceivably die for a good person) throws the divine love into relief: human love has an upper limit; divine love in Christ has none.

verseByVerse.quote: but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The demonstration of love is not a word but an event: 'God shows his love for us' in the death of his Son. And the timing is everything: 'while we were still sinners.' Not after we had cleaned ourselves up, not after we had proven our worthiness, not after we had made the first move toward God. The cross is God's initiative at humanity's lowest point. Stott called this the most astonishing fact in the universe: the Creator dying for the creature, the Holy One dying for sinners, at the moment of their maximum unworthiness.

verseByVerse.quote: Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul uses a 'how much more' argument from the greater to the lesser. If God accomplished the harder thing — reconciling enemies, justifying the ungodly, through the death of his Son — how much more certain is the easier thing: keeping and completing the salvation of those who are now his friends? The ongoing salvation is secured 'by his life' — the resurrection and intercession of the living Christ. Justification is the foundation; glorification is the guaranteed superstructure. What God began in the cross, the risen Christ will bring to completion.

verseByVerse.quote: More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final joy is the greatest: not merely rejoicing in blessings or in hope or even in the escape from wrath, but rejoicing in God himself. Reconciliation — the restoration of the fundamental relationship between the creature and the Creator — is now ours 'through our Lord Jesus Christ.' The mediator is named again: all access to the Father, all joy in God, all reconciliation comes through the one who bore the enmity and ended the war at the cost of his own life. This is the gospel as doxology.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Death in Adam, Life in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The argument that begins in v. 12 is the most theologically ambitious in the entire letter. Paul steps back from the individual experience of justification and places it within a cosmic, historical framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose representative actions determined the status and destiny of everyone who belongs to them. This is the doctrine of federal headship — the two-Adam theology that is foundational to the Reformed understanding of both sin and salvation.

The parallel is deliberate and asymmetrical. Adam sinned; condemnation and death spread to all. Christ obeyed; righteousness and life are given to all who are in Him. But the parallel is asymmetrical because grace exceeds sin in every dimension: "the free gift is not like the trespass" (v. 15). The trespass brought condemnation; the gift brings justification for many trespasses. Adam's one sin brought death; Christ's one act of righteousness brings the free gift of life. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (v. 20). The gospel is not simply the repair of the damage done by Adam; it is a new creation that surpasses Eden.

The phrase "just as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 21) is the conclusion to which the whole argument has been driving. Sin had a reign — a dominion, a kingdom of death. Grace now has a counter-reign — a dominion of life and righteousness. The believer has been transferred from one kingdom to the other. Adam is no longer her representative head; Christ is. She bears the condemnation of neither Adam's sin (fully atoned) nor her own (fully forgiven). She stands under the reign of grace, heading toward the eternal life that is the gift of her new federal head.
verseByVerse.theology:
Federal Headship: The Solidarity of Adam and Christ

Romans 5:12–21 is the biblical foundation of the Reformed doctrine of original sin and the imputation of Adam's guilt. Paul teaches that death spread to all because all sinned in Adam — not merely by imitating his example, but by being represented by him. Adam was the covenantal head of humanity; his act was our act in the only sense that matters covenantally. This is why all die, even infants who have not sinned in the way Adam sinned (v. 14). The parallel with Christ is the point: just as we were condemned in Adam by imputation, we are justified in Christ by imputation. The same covenantal logic that makes us sinners in Adam makes us righteous in Christ. You cannot reject one side of the parallel without undermining the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Adam-Christ typology was deeply embedded in Jewish theology of Paul's day — the figure of Adam as the representative of humanity was well established. Paul takes this shared theological framework and uses it to explain both the universality of sin and the universality of the gospel's offer: as Adam's headship was universal (all who are human bear his guilt), so Christ's headship is available to all (all who are in Him receive His righteousness). Now: The doctrine of original sin is the one Christian teaching that can be empirically verified by reading any newspaper. Every generation produces fresh evidence that something has gone profoundly wrong with the human race at its root. Romans 5:12–21 names it: Adam. And then offers the only remedy: Christ. The diagnosis and the cure are inseparable.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul introduces the Adam-Christ parallel that will dominate the chapter. Through one man — Adam — sin entered the world's story, and death entered as its consequence. 'Death spread to all men because all sinned' — the precise relationship between Adam's sin and universal human guilt has generated centuries of theological debate, but Paul's point is clear: Adam's action and our condition are inseparably linked. The addition that sin existed before the Mosaic law (and was therefore real sin) demonstrates that law is not the definition of sin but only its written codification.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.
verseByVerse.commentary: Death reigned — not merely occurred, not merely threatened, but exercised dominion — over the entire period from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not received an explicit divine command as Adam had. This universal reign of death demonstrates that something more than personal transgression is at work: there is a solidarity of ruin, a shared condition of mortality that precedes individual moral failure. And Adam is 'a type of the one who was to come' — the one whose solidarity with humanity would work in the opposite direction, bringing life where Adam brought death.

verseByVerse.quote: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul insists three times that the parallel is not a simple equivalence: the free gift is 'not like the trespass.' The asymmetry is this: Adam's one act undid one state of righteousness; Christ's one act overcame the accumulated mass of many trespasses. The direction of the imbalance is grace's direction — grace abounds beyond the measure of ruin. Condemnation came from one act; justification comes despite many. The scale tips toward grace. Sproul: 'Where sin abounded, grace super-abounded — the surplus is always on the side of mercy.'

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The reversal is total: where death once reigned as king over humanity, those who receive the abundance of grace will themselves reign in life. The direction of sovereignty is inverted. Union with Adam meant being ruled by death; union with Christ means ruling with life. The 'abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness' received by faith transforms subjects of death into co-regents of life. This is the eschatological destiny of the justified: not merely survival but glorified reign, sharing in the victory of the Last Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. — Romans 5:18–19
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallel is now stated with maximum clarity: one trespass → condemnation for all / one act of righteousness → justification for all. The "one act of righteousness" refers most naturally to the obedience of Christ's entire life culminating in the cross — the perfect, comprehensive obedience that the law required and that Adam failed to render. Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed — at every point, at every pressure, to the ultimate degree of giving His life.

"Made sinners" and "made righteous" are legal or covenantal terms — not descriptions of personal moral character but of standing before God. Those in Adam are constituted sinners by their representative's act; those in Christ are constituted righteous by their representative's act. This is the doctrine of imputation operating symmetrically: the same mechanism that makes us guilty in Adam makes us righteous in Christ. To reject one side of the parallel is to undermine the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 5:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more" — this sentence has fuelled both hope and misunderstanding across two millennia. The misunderstanding: it licenses more sinning to get more grace (which Paul will demolish immediately in 6:1). The hope: no depth of human sin is beyond the reach of divine grace. The greatest sinner is not beyond the scope of the gospel. The most spectacular prodigal is not past the point at which grace can abound.

The reign of grace through righteousness is the great theme of Romans 6–8: the justified person does not merely receive a changed verdict; she enters a new dominion. She is no longer under the reign of sin and death — no longer defined by Adam's inheritance or her own accumulated failures. She is under the reign of grace, moving toward eternal life, claimed and kept by the God who abounds.

6.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.overview:
Romans 6 opens with the most dangerous question the gospel generates: "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?" If grace covers all sin, and more sin produces more grace, why not sin freely? Paul's answer — "By no means!" — is the most vehement denial in the letter. The question misunderstands both the nature of grace and the nature of the union with Christ that is the foundation of the justified life.

The answer Paul gives is not primarily ethical (you should not sin) but theological (you cannot sin in the way that question imagines, because of who you now are in Christ). Union with Christ in His death and resurrection has changed the believer's fundamental status with respect to sin. She has died to it. It no longer has jurisdiction over her. The command that follows — "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" — is not a technique for sin management but a theological reality to be reckoned with and lived from.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — United with Christ in Death and Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's answer to the antinomian question is grounded in baptism — not as a magical ritual but as the enacted sign of the believer's union with Christ in His death and resurrection. "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?" Baptism is the visible declaration of an invisible reality: the believer has been co-crucified with Christ, co-buried with Him, and co-raised with Him into newness of life. These are not future aspirations; they are present realities that define who the Christian is.

The key concept is "our old self was crucified with him" (v. 6) — the person we were in Adam, defined by sin's dominion, is dead. Not sick, not weakened, not being rehabilitated — dead. Sin still exists in the believer (7:14–25 will be painfully honest about this), but sin no longer reigns. The one who is in Christ has been transferred out of sin's kingdom and into grace's kingdom. She is not a sinner desperately trying to become a saint; she is a saint who still struggles with sin. The identity has changed, even while the struggle continues.

The imperatives of vv. 11–14 flow from the indicatives of vv. 1–10. "Consider yourselves dead to sin" (v. 11) — reckon it, take it into account, live from this reality. "Do not let sin reign" (v. 12) — the fact that sin no longer must reign does not mean the battle is over; it means the battle is now winnable. "Present yourselves to God" (v. 13) — the person whose old self has been crucified with Christ is now free to offer herself as a living sacrifice to the God she could not truly serve before.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ: The Foundation of Sanctification

Romans 6 grounds sanctification in union with Christ, not in moral effort or spiritual discipline alone. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that justification and sanctification, though distinct, are inseparable — both are fruits of union with Christ. John Murray's landmark study Redemption Accomplished and Applied showed that union with Christ is not an add-on to the Christian life but its very foundation: every blessing of salvation flows from being in Christ. We are justified in Christ, sanctified in Christ, glorified in Christ. The call to holiness in Romans 6 is not the demand to earn what we have not yet received; it is the call to live consistently with what is already true of us in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The antinomian objection Paul addresses — "let us sin that grace may abound" — was apparently a real misreading of his gospel in his own day (v. 1 and 3:8). Some had heard his message of free grace and concluded that moral behaviour was irrelevant. Paul's reply is not to retreat into moralism but to deepen the gospel: the same grace that justifies also transforms. Grace is not a license; it is a power that liberates from the dominion of sin. Now: The same objection recurs whenever grace is preached with full biblical clarity. The person who is never accused of antinomianism by those who prefer a works-based gospel has probably not yet preached grace clearly enough. But Paul's answer stands: grace does not produce moral indifference; it produces the only genuine moral transformation available — the transformation of a person who has died and risen with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By no means!' (mē genoito) — the strongest negation available in Greek. The question itself reveals how explosive the doctrine of grace is: if justification is entirely free, apart from works, does it not remove the incentive for holiness? Paul's answer is not a legal constraint ('you must not sin') but an ontological impossibility ('how can we?'). Those who have died to sin cannot continue living in it, not because they are compelled from outside but because their very relationship to sin has been fundamentally altered by union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary: Baptism into Christ is baptism into his death — union with Christ in his representative dying. 'Buried with him' — the burial is significant: it marks the definitiveness of the death, the irreversibility of the transition. But the burial is not the end: the purpose clause is resurrection: 'in order that... we too might walk in newness of life.' The new life is not an aspiration but a present reality — the resurrection of Christ has created a new existence into which believers have been incorporated. Walking in it is the daily actualization of what has already occurred definitionally.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: Union with Christ in death guarantees union with Christ in resurrection — the logic is inexorable. The 'old self' (palaios anthrōpos) — the entire pre-conversion person defined by Adam's solidarity — was crucified with Christ. This is not a process to be achieved but an event that occurred when Christ died: the representative death that abolished the old humanity's defining relationship to sin. The purpose: that 'the body of sin might be brought to nothing' — not destroyed physically but rendered powerless, deprived of dominion.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One who has died has been set free from sin' — this is a principle: death terminates legal obligation. A dead man owes no more taxes, stands before no more courts. The believer who has died with Christ is therefore legally freed from sin's claim. And this death with Christ carries its own guarantee: if we have died with him, we will also live with him. The resurrection life is not a separate benefit to be hoped for; it is the inseparable other side of the death that has already occurred.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The resurrection of Christ is permanent — 'death no longer has dominion over him.' He died to sin 'once for all' (ephapax) — his engagement with sin in death was total, definitive, unrepeatable. There is no second death for Christ, no renewed exposure to sin's domain. He now lives entirely and permanently to God. This is the shape of the believer's new existence: having died to sin once (in solidarity with Christ's death), living now to God — entirely, permanently, in the new sphere where God is the only horizon.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One who has died has been set free from sin' — death terminates legal obligation. A dead man owes no more debts, stands before no more courts. The believer who has died with Christ is therefore legally freed from sin's claim. And this death carries its own guarantee: death with Christ inseparably means life with Christ. The resurrection life is not a separate hope to be separately sought; it is the inseparable other side of the death that has already occurred.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The resurrection of Christ is permanent and unrepeatable — 'death no longer has dominion over him.' He died to sin 'once for all' (ephapax): his engagement with sin's domain was total, definitive, complete. There is no second death for Christ, no renewed exposure. He now lives entirely to God. This is the shape of the believer's existence mirrored in the pattern of the head: having died to sin once, living now entirely to God — permanently, irreversibly, in the sphere where God is the only horizon.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Consider yourselves' (logizesthe) — the same verb used of imputation. Paul calls believers to reckon as true what is already true: 'You are dead to sin. Believe it about yourself.' This is the indicative that grounds the imperative. Because you are dead to sin and alive to God in Christ, do not let sin reign. The command presupposes freedom — sin cannot compel; it can only attempt to reign where it has been dethroned. The mortal body is not itself sinful (Paul will insist on bodily resurrection), but it is the arena in which the daily battle over sin's attempted restoration is fought.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Instruments for righteousness' — the same body that sin once conscripted for unrighteousness is now to be offered to God as the tool of his purposes. The present tense of 'do not present' contrasted with the aorist of 'present yourselves to God' suggests: stop the ongoing habit of yielding to sin, and make the definitive once-for-all surrender to God. 'Sin will have no dominion over you' — this is not a command but a promise, grounded in the believer's standing: not under law (where sin exploits condemnation) but under grace (where sin has been dethroned).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Slaves of Righteousness: Freedom and Its Direction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question of v. 15 replays the question of v. 1 in a new key: "Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace?" This is the libertarian version of the antinomian objection — if the law is not our master, then surely we are free to do anything. Paul's answer is again a flat denial, followed by a theological argument: freedom from sin does not mean freedom from all master; it means a change of master. Every human being serves either sin or righteousness — there is no neutral ground, no autonomous freedom that is subject to nothing.

The language of slavery runs throughout the passage and is deliberately shocking. Sin is a slave-master. Righteousness is a slave-master. The difference is in the direction: slavery to sin leads to death; slavery to righteousness leads to life and holiness. The Christian is not more free than the unbeliever in the sense of being subject to nothing; she is more free in the sense that she now serves the master whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light — the master whose service is perfect freedom.

The concluding verse is one of the most famous in the letter: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The contrast between wages and gift is the contrast between law and gospel. Death is what sin earns — a wage paid in proportion to the work done. Eternal life is what God gives — a gift, free, unearned, proportionate not to the recipient's merit but to the giver's generosity. The entire letter is in this sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace and the New Obedience

Romans 6:15–23 establishes that grace does not produce lawlessness but a new and deeper obedience — obedience that flows from a changed heart rather than a legal compulsion. The Reformers distinguished between the "old obedience" (driven by fear of punishment and desire for reward) and the "new obedience" (driven by love for God and gratitude for grace). Calvin was particularly insistent that the justified Christian is not released from obedience but liberated for it — the law now functions as a guide for the regenerate, not as a court that condemns. The third use of the law: the Christian, freed from condemnation, embraces the law as the expression of the will of the God she loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's slavery metaphor was immediately intelligible to a first-century audience in which slavery was the defining social institution. Every person knew what it meant to be owned by a master, to have their labour and their body subject to another's will. Paul's redeployment of this metaphor is arresting: you were a slave before, and you are a slave now — the only question is whose slave you are. The liberated Christian is not autonomous; she is re-owned, by a Master who purchased her with His own blood. Now: The modern West prizes autonomy above almost everything — the right to define oneself, to determine one's own values, to answer to no authority beyond the self. Romans 6 is a direct challenge to this: the autonomous self is a myth. Every person serves something — appetite, ambition, approval, comfort, identity. The gospel does not offer escape from all masters; it offers the only master worth serving.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
verseByVerse.commentary: The antinomian question returns in a slightly different form (cf. 6:1), and receives the same categorical answer. Paul's counter-argument is the logic of slavery: whatever you obey, that is your master. Freedom from law does not mean freedom from all authority — it means transfer to a new master. The only question is which master you serve: sin, whose wages are death, or obedience, whose end is righteousness. Grace does not create a moral vacuum; it creates the freedom to serve the right master.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Thanks be to God' — a spontaneous doxology in the middle of an argument. The transfer of masters is an act of divine grace, not human decision: God is the one who freed them and transferred them. 'Obedient from the heart' — the new obedience is not external compliance but internal transformation. The heart has been reoriented; the submission is genuine. 'The standard of teaching to which you were committed' — the apostolic gospel is the mold into which grace has pressed them. Slavery to righteousness is the paradoxical freedom of those who have found the master who made them for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul apologizes for the slavery metaphor ('I am speaking in human terms') — no metaphor fully captures the reality of the Christian's relationship to God. But the metaphor illuminates by contrast: in the old life, members were freely offered to impurity, and impurity led not to satisfaction but to more lawlessness in an escalating spiral. The new life reverses the spiral: righteousness, presented as a slave's service, leads to sanctification — the progressive reorientation of the whole person toward God. The former 'freedom from righteousness' was the most enslaving condition possible.

verseByVerse.quote: But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul invites a backward look: what did sin actually produce? Shame — the fruit that leaves you unable to look at what you have done. And the ultimate end: death. The contrast with the present is stark: freedom from sin, slavery to God, fruit that leads to sanctification, and at the end, eternal life. The same framework (master → service → fruit → end) produces radically different results depending on the master. Eternal life is not earned by the service — it is the gracious end to which God brings those who belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 6:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
The economy of sin and the economy of grace are placed side by side in one unforgettable sentence. Wages are earned; gifts are given. Death is what sin produces — the inevitable outcome of a life lived under sin's dominion, the just consequence of rebellion against the source of all life. Eternal life is what God gives — not what we produce, not what we earn, not what we deserve. It is a gift, and it comes through a Person: Jesus Christ our Lord.

The specificity of "in Christ Jesus our Lord" is crucial. Eternal life is not a free-floating spiritual benefit that God distributes to deserving people. It is located in a Person — the Person who is Himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). To receive eternal life is to receive Christ; to have Christ is to have eternal life. This is why John can say that whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). Life is not a commodity God can give; it is a relationship with the God who is life.

7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 is one of the most debated chapters in the New Testament. The first six verses use the analogy of marriage to explain the Christian's release from the law — just as death dissolves a marriage, so the death of the old self has dissolved the law's claim on the believer. Verses 7–25 then address the relationship between the law and sin in a passage of such raw psychological honesty that it has divided interpreters for centuries: is Paul describing his experience before or after his conversion?

The Reformed tradition, following Luther, Calvin, and Lloyd-Jones, has generally argued that vv. 7–25 describe the experience of the regenerate person — not as the normal steady state of the mature Christian, but as the honest account of the ongoing struggle that even the believer has with indwelling sin. The person who says "I delight in the law of God in my inner being" (v. 22) is not an unregenerate person; the unregenerate person has no such delight. The chapter is not a counsel of despair but a radical honesty about the nature of the Christian struggle — which ends, in v. 25, with the triumphant answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul uses the analogy of marriage to make a point about the law's jurisdiction. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, the Christian has "died" to the law through her union with Christ's death — she is no longer bound to the law as a system of earning and condemnation. She is now married to another — to Christ who was raised from the dead — so that she might bear fruit for God.

The point is not that the law is bad (v. 7 will explicitly deny this) but that the law was never the instrument of life. Under the law's jurisdiction, the sinful passions "aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (v. 5). This does not mean the law created those sinful passions; it means that the sinful nature, encountering prohibition, is provoked — not helped — by the law. The law reveals and aggravates what is already there; it cannot remove it.

But now — freed from the law, joined to Christ — the Christian serves "in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (v. 6). This is not antinomianism; it is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 — the new covenant in which the law is written on the heart by the Spirit, not merely imposed from without by the letter. The motive for obedience has changed: from fear of penalty to love of the God who has shown such grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

The believer's death to the law (vv. 4, 6) has been the source of great misunderstanding. Paul is not teaching that the Christian is released from the moral content of the law — he will demonstrate in chapters 12–15 that the redeemed life is the life of love, which is the fulfilment of the law (13:8–10). He is teaching that the believer's relationship to the law has changed: no longer subject to it as a court that condemns, the Christian is now free to embrace its moral demands as the expression of the will of the God she loves. Calvin's third use of the law: a guide for the regenerate, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The marriage analogy was immediately accessible to Paul's Jewish readers, for whom marriage law was well understood. The death that dissolves the marriage — the death of the old self in union with Christ's death — was the theologically startling element. Paul is saying: you belong to a new husband now. The old master (law as condemning power) is dead to you; the new master (Christ) is alive to you. Serve him accordingly. Now: Many Christians live as though they are still married to the law — haunted by condemnation, driven by religious duty, exhausted by the performance of obligation. Romans 7:1–6 is the declaration of liberty: you have died to that system. You are joined to Christ. Serve him from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul introduces a legal principle: law's authority terminates at death. He illustrates from marriage law, which his readers who 'know the law' would recognize immediately. The binding force of the marriage covenant is real and serious — but it is dissolved by death. This is not an attempt to allegorize marriage but to establish the principle of death as the termination of legal obligation, a principle he will apply to the believer's relationship to the Mosaic law.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary: The illustration completes its point: the law that bound her is no longer operative once her husband has died — and the act that would have been adultery (belonging to another) is now perfectly lawful. Death has changed everything. Paul will apply this to the believer's death to the law through union with Christ: what would have been lawlessness (living outside the law's jurisdiction) is now freedom, because the death that terminates the old relationship has occurred in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary: The application reverses the illustration's terms: it is not the husband (the law) who has died but the believer — 'you have died to the law through the body of Christ.' Death with Christ terminated the believer's legal obligation to the law as a covenant of works. The purpose is not lawlessness but a new marriage: belonging to the risen Christ, bearing fruit for God. The former state under law is described starkly: sinful passions, aroused by the law (which will be unpacked in vv. 7–13), bearing fruit for death. The law could diagnose and inflame but never cure.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Released' — the same word used of the widow freed from the marriage law. The believer has been discharged from the law as a binding covenant of death. The contrast is between two modes of service: the old way of the written code (external rule producing only condemnation and failure) and the new way of the Spirit (internal transformation producing genuine obedience from the heart). The law written on stone is replaced by the law written by the Spirit on the heart — the fulfillment of Jeremiah's new covenant promise (31:31–34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" Paul's defence of the law is passionate and complete: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is not the law; the problem is sin — which used the good commandment as a foothold for its own agenda. When the commandment "you shall not covet" entered Paul's consciousness, it awakened the very covetousness it forbade. Not because the commandment was defective, but because sin is so pervasive that even the confrontation with prohibition provokes the prohibited desire.

The famous passage beginning in v. 14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" — is the most honest description of the experience of indwelling sin in all of Scripture. Whether Paul is describing pre-conversion or post-conversion experience has been debated exhaustively. The weight of the evidence — the delight in God's law (v. 22), the willing of the good (v. 18), the self-awareness of the conflict — points to the regenerate person, not the unregenerate.

The climax of the chapter is both a cry and a triumph: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (vv. 24–25). The cry of anguish is honest; the gratitude that follows is immediate. Paul does not wallow in the wretchedness. He knows the answer. He has the answer. The very struggle he describes is the evidence that the Spirit is at work — because the person without the Spirit does not experience this conflict; she simply does what sin desires. The one who hates what she does and loves the law of God in her inner being is alive in Christ, even while she wars against the flesh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine that sanctification is a lifelong struggle, not a crisis experience of eradication. John Wesley and the Holiness tradition argued for the possibility of entire sanctification — the complete eradication of the sinful nature — in this life. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, has insisted that indwelling sin remains until glorification. This is not defeatism but realism: the Christian who understands this will not be surprised or destroyed by the ongoing struggle. She will be equipped to fight it with the means God has provided — the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the community of believers — rather than pretending it does not exist or despairing when it does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The experience Paul describes in vv. 14–25 had a parallel in Stoic philosophy — Ovid's famous line: "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse." But the Stoic solution (more reason, more discipline, more willpower) is precisely what Paul finds inadequate. The problem is not ignorance; it is the power of indwelling sin that reason alone cannot overcome. The solution is not philosophy; it is the liberating power of "Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has experienced Romans 7 — who has tried harder, prayed more, committed afresh, and still found the same sins returning — is not a failure. She is a normal Christian, living in the honest tension between the new self and the old, between the delight in God's law and the drag of indwelling sin. The answer is not more effort; it is more Christ. Chapter 8 is the answer to chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The law is sin? By no means!' — the law is holy (v. 12), but it has an unexpected and alarming effect: it arouses what it forbids. Sin, Paul says, 'seizes an opportunity' (aphormē — a military bridgehead) through the commandment. Prohibition awakens desire; the forbidden becomes attractive precisely because it is forbidden. This is not the law's fault — it is sin's cunning. The law reveals the command; sin uses the knowledge of the command as the occasion for transgression. Apart from the law, sin 'lies dead' — not absent, but dormant, unexposed.

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Whether Paul describes his own pre-conversion experience, Israel's experience at Sinai, or Adam's experience in the garden (or all three simultaneously), the pattern is clear: arrival of the commandment meant death for the one who transgressed it. The commandment 'promised life' — this was its design (Leviticus 18:5: 'keep my statutes and live'). But sin intercepted the promise and turned the instrument of life into the occasion of death. This is the tragedy of the law's relationship to fallen humanity: the perfect tool in the hands of a broken workman.

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary: The echo of Genesis 3 is unmistakable: 'sin... deceived me.' The serpent used God's prohibition to entice; sin uses God's commandment to destroy. But the culprit is sin, not the law. The law is 'holy and righteous and good' — Paul is emphatic and threefold. The problem is not in the physician's prescription; the problem is in the patient's condition. To blame the law for producing death is to blame the mirror for the ugliness it reflects.

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary: The law did not cause death; sin hijacked the law to produce death — and in doing so, exposed itself as sin. The law's function in this process is diagnostic and revelatory: it makes sin 'sinful beyond measure,' forces it into the open, strips away the excuse of ignorance. The commandment is the instrument by which sin is unmasked in its true character: not mere human weakness, but active, cunning rebellion against the holy God. The law that cannot save has an indispensable role: it shows us exactly what we need saving from.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary: The famous and debated passage of Romans 7:14–25. Whether this describes Paul's pre-conversion struggle, his ongoing Christian experience, or a rhetorical persona, the psychology is unmistakably precise. 'Sold under sin' — a slave in the market, owned by a master he despises. The wrenching self-division ('I do not do what I want, but the very thing I hate') is the experience of a person whose moral knowledge and moral performance have come apart. He knows the good; he wills the good; and yet he does otherwise. This is not mere weakness — it is captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary: There is an argument in the self-division: if I do what I do not want, my very unwillingness is a testimony to the goodness of the law I am violating. The conscience that feels guilt is itself a witness to the moral order it is breaking. And the distinction between 'I' and 'sin that dwells within me' is not an evasion of responsibility but a diagnosis: there is an alien power operating within the self, a power that is not the true self but that the true self cannot expel. This is the experience of indwelling sin — not the whole person, but a power the person has not yet been able to defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh' — Paul carefully qualifies: not in me as a whole, but in my flesh — the unredeemed, sin-corrupted nature that persists even in the believer. The desire is present; the ability is absent. This is the frustration of the regenerate conscience trapped in unredeemed flesh: seeing clearly what ought to be done, willing it genuinely, and yet finding the performance elusive. Lloyd-Jones noted that this description is impossible for an unregenerate person — only the regenerate person has the spiritual understanding to see the gap between what is and what ought to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: The observation crystallizes into a general 'law' (principle, pattern): evil is always close at hand when the good is desired. The presence of the desire for good does not displace the presence of evil — they coexist in painful proximity within the same person. This is the experience that moves the passage toward its climax of desperation: not occasional failure but a structural condition, a law as reliable as gravity. The only exit from this condition is not self-improvement but divine deliverance — which is exactly where the argument arrives in v. 25 and chapter 8.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary: The inner conflict is now described as warfare: two laws (principles) in combat within the same person. The inner person delights in God's law — this is the deepest self, the self created and renewed by God. But the members (the body as the site of physical desire and habit) house another law that wages war and takes captive. 'Makes me captive' — the language of a prisoner of war: defeated, bound, carried off. The delight of the inner person is real; so is the captivity. This is not hypocrisy but the genuine anguish of a divided person.

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wretched man that I am!' — the cry of genuine desperation, the bankruptcy of every human program for self-improvement. The question is not 'what will deliver me?' but 'who?' — deliverance requires a person, a deliverer, not a technique or a discipline. And the answer erupts before the argument demands it: 'Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!' The deliverer has come. Chapter 8 will unfold what this looks like; but the doxology breaks out here because the gospel cannot be contained. The summary of v. 25b acknowledges that the conflict described is real and ongoing — but the outcome is certain, because the deliverer is named.

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Romans 8 is the mountain peak of the New Testament. Commentators across twenty centuries have reached for superlatives and still found them inadequate. Luther said it deserved to be committed to memory by every Christian. Lloyd-Jones preached sixty sermons on it. John Stott called it "the most devotional chapter in the Bible." It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with "no separation" — and between those two impossibilities of loss, it contains the fullest and most glorious account of the Christian life available in Scripture: the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation, the golden chain of redemption, and the love of God from which nothing in the universe can separate us.

The movement of the chapter is from liberation (vv. 1–17) through present suffering (vv. 18–27) to eternal security (vv. 28–39). In each movement, the Spirit is central: He liberates (vv. 1–11), He adopts (vv. 14–17), He intercedes (vv. 26–27). And over all of it stands the sovereign love of a God who foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and will glorify — a chain that has never had a broken link and never will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." Eight words in English, two in Greek (ouden katakrima), and the whole of the gospel's comfort is here. Not less condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. No condemnation. The verdict is absolute, unconditional, and permanent. It rests not on the quality of the believer's life on any given day but on the finished work of Christ and the irreversible union with Him by faith.

The reason for the "no condemnation" is the "law of the Spirit of life" which has set the believer free from "the law of sin and death" (v. 2). This is not two different legal codes but two different powers — the power of the Spirit that gives life versus the power of sin that produces death. Christ condemned sin in the flesh (v. 3) — He bore its penalty, exhausted its power, stripped it of its right to condemn — so that the Spirit-empowered believer might fulfil the righteous requirement of the law (v. 4).

The contrast between "flesh" and "Spirit" in vv. 5–11 is not between body and soul — Paul is not a Gnostic. It is between life oriented around the self and its capacities (flesh) and life oriented around God and His Spirit (Spirit). The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. The Christian is not defined by the flesh but by the Spirit — "you, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you" (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Definitive Justification and Ongoing Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the permanent foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The condemnation that does not exist for those in Christ is not merely past (sins before conversion) but total: nothing from the past, present, or future can generate condemnation for the one who is in Christ. This is because justification is not a process but an event — a forensic declaration that has been made and cannot be unmade. The Christian may sin grievously; she is not beyond condemnation but she is not in danger of final condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glorification.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jewish legal system that Paul's readers knew well had a concept of condemnation — the verdict of guilty rendered by a court against one who had violated the law. Paul takes this forensic language and applies it to the ultimate court: the tribunal of God. The verdict of "no condemnation" is the legal declaration of the divine Judge that the case is closed, the penalty has been paid, and the accused walks free — permanently. Now: Countless Christians live under a cloud of functional condemnation — not doubting their doctrinal justification but unable to feel free, perpetually haunted by past sins, unable to receive grace without qualifying it. Romans 8:1 is the word that cuts through all of this: not less condemnation, not reduced condemnation — none. Take it in. Live from it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In Christ Jesus" — the location of the believer is the ground of her freedom from condemnation. She is not in herself, where condemnation would be entirely appropriate. She is in Christ — hidden in Him, clothed in His righteousness, participating in His verdict of "righteous" before the Father. The condemnation fell on Christ at the cross; it cannot fall again on those who are found in Him.

"The law of the Spirit of life" versus "the law of sin and death" — two powers contending for the human person. Before conversion, the law of sin and death had total jurisdiction: sin indwelled, death reigned, condemnation was the only verdict possible. After conversion — in Christ, by the Spirit — a stronger power has entered and set the prisoner free. The chains are broken, not by the prisoner's effort, but by the liberating power of the Spirit of God.

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 3–4 are the theological engine of the entire chapter. The law could not accomplish what God required — not because the law was defective but because the flesh was too weak, too thoroughly under sin's power, to respond to the law's demands. So God did what the law could not do: He sent His own Son. The phrase "in the likeness of sinful flesh" is carefully worded: Christ took on genuine human flesh (not a spiritual appearance) while remaining without sin. He came where sin had its domain — in human flesh — in order to condemn sin there, in its own territory.

"Condemned sin in the flesh" — at the cross, the sentence that sin deserved was executed. Not in a sinner, but in the sinless Son who bore sinners' sin.
