When Paul says "bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2), the law of Christ is precisely this: the pattern of the one who bore what He did not owe so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" — was not an abstract aspiration. The Roman church had real divisions: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people from different social classes and national backgrounds. The one voice of praise was the visible, social miracle that would demonstrate to the watching city of Rome that something genuinely new had entered the world. Now: The unity of diverse believers in genuine, cross-cultural, cross-social worship is still the most powerful apologetic the church has available. A community of people who have every reason to be divided — by race, class, culture, education, politics — worshipping together with one voice glorifies the God whose gospel is the only power that creates such unity.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We who are strong have an obligation' — Paul identifies himself with the strong, but the identification carries a duty, not a privilege. The strong do not have the right to lord their freedom over the weak; they have the obligation to bear the weak's failings. 'Not to please ourselves' — the organizing principle of the Christian life is not self-gratification but neighbor-good. Keller: 'The gospel produces people whose first question in any situation is not what do I get but what does my neighbor need.'

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological ground of the ethical command: Christ is the pattern. He did not please himself — the Son of God voluntarily relinquished his divine prerogatives to take the form of a servant and bear human reproach. The citation from Psalm 69:9 (applied to Christ throughout the New Testament) shows that the Messiah absorbed the hostility directed at God himself. If the strong are to bear the failings of the weak, the pattern is Christ bearing infinitely more than any human failing demands. The cross is both the motive and the measure of Christian self-giving.

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction' — one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of the continuing relevance of the Old Testament for the church. The Scriptures produce endurance (by showing how God has sustained his people through every crisis) and encouragement (by confirming that his purposes do not fail), and together these produce hope. The God who is the source of these qualities in Scripture is also the one prayed to for the unity of the community — the same character is being appealed to.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'With one voice' — the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in worship is the visible demonstration of the gospel's power. The goal of the ethical instructions of chapters 14–15 is not merely social harmony but doxological: together glorifying God. The ground of mutual welcome is Christ's welcome: 'as Christ has welcomed you.' The welcome Christ extended was at infinite cost to himself and to those who were, by nature, strangers and enemies. The welcome the community is to extend is modeled on and energized by the welcome it has received.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary: Christ's ministry had a dual purpose: to confirm the promises to Israel (showing God's faithfulness to the patriarchs) and to extend mercy to the Gentiles (showing God's grace beyond the covenant). Both Jew and Gentile are served by the one Christ, though through different aspects of his saving work: covenant fulfillment for the Jew, mercy extension for the Gentile. The quotation from Psalm 18:49 (David praising God among the nations) becomes, in Christ, the Messiah incorporating the Gentiles into his own praise of the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: And again it is said, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Deuteronomy 32:43 and Psalm 117:1 both envision the Gentiles joining Israel in praise of the God of Israel. Moses and the Psalmist saw it; Paul has watched it unfold. The Gentiles are not replacing Israel in worship — they are joining Israel, praising the same God with the same voice, in fulfillment of the ancient vision. The unity of Jewish and Gentile praise is itself the eschatological sign that the Messiah has come and accomplished his work.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 11:10 — the Messiah from Jesse's line arising to rule the Gentiles, in whom the nations will hope. This is the christological center of Paul's scriptural argument: all four citations (Psalm 18, Deuteronomy 32, Psalm 117, Isaiah 11) converge on Christ as the one through whom the Gentiles enter the praise and hope of Israel's God. The ancient promise is present reality; the present reality confirms the promise was never merely national but always cosmic in its reach.

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
The benediction of v. 13 is one of the most complete prayers in the New Testament. The God of hope — not merely the God who gives hope but the God who is its source and guarantor — fills: not trickles, not portions, but fills. All joy — not qualified, not conditional joy but full joy. Peace in believing — the peace that is the fruit of faith in the God who justifies, adopts, and keeps. And the Spirit — the divine person through whose power hope overflows rather than merely exists.

The prayer is for abundance: "abound in hope." Not enough hope to get by. Not sufficient hope to endure. Abounding hope — more hope than circumstances justify, more hope than reason supports, hope that overflows because the Spirit who gives it is infinite. This is what the gospel produces in those who have truly received it: an excess of hope that the world cannot explain and death cannot extinguish.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now turns from theology and pastoral exhortation to autobiography and travel plans — and the transition is less abrupt than it appears. His account of his apostolic ministry is itself a miniature theology of mission. He describes himself as a minister (leitourgos — a cultic, priestly term) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, performing the priestly service of the gospel of God, offering the Gentiles as an acceptable offering, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (v. 16). The mission to the Gentiles is not merely evangelistic strategy; it is priestly worship — the bringing of the nations as an offering to God.

The scope of Paul's completed mission (vv. 19–21) is staggering: from Jerusalem to Illyricum (modern-day Croatia), he has "fulfilled the gospel of Christ." Not because every person has heard it but because he has planted the gospel in strategic centres throughout the eastern Mediterranean, from which the word can spread into every surrounding region. His ambition going forward is equally characteristic: not to build on another man's foundation, but to preach where Christ has not yet been named. The pioneer missionary impulse is written into the logic of the commission.

The prayer request of vv. 30–33 is one of the most moving passages in Paul's letters. He asks the Roman church to "strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf" — the word for "strive together" (sunagōnizomai) is an athletic term, the cooperation of two wrestlers straining together. Prayer is work, and Paul wants co-labourers in it. He asks for three things: deliverance from unbelievers in Judea, acceptance of his offering by the Jerusalem church, and the joy of reaching Rome. Two of the three will be granted in unexpected ways; the Rome visit will happen, but in chains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as Priestly Worship

Romans 15:16 is one of the most theologically rich descriptions of apostolic mission in the New Testament. Paul images his Gentile mission as priestly service — the offering of the nations to God as a sacrifice acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Spirit. This means that evangelism is not merely a strategy for church growth or a duty to be discharged; it is an act of worship, the gathering of the nations to lay them as a living offering before the God who created and redeemed them. This priestly vision of mission has sustained every great missionary movement in the Reformed tradition, from Calvin's Geneva sending missionaries to France, to William Carey going to India, to the countless sent ones who have carried the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's completed mission from Jerusalem to Illyricum represents perhaps fifteen years of gruelling apostolic labour — multiple missionary journeys, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, cold and hunger. The nonchalance with which he refers to "having fulfilled" the gospel in this vast region is the confidence of a man who has done what he was sent to do and is already looking at the next frontier. Now: The pioneer missionary impulse of v. 20 — to preach where Christ has not been named — remains the highest calling in the church's mission. There are still places, peoples, and communities where the name of Christ has not been proclaimed. The obligation Paul felt is the obligation the church still carries, until all nations have heard.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul closes the doctrinal body of the letter with pastoral generosity: he is not writing to a deficient church but reminding a capable one. 'Full of goodness, filled with all knowledge' — the Roman church is mature. The boldness of the letter is not superiority but apostolic responsibility: the 'grace given me by God' (the apostolic commission) creates an obligation to speak even to those who already know, because the gospel is too important to assume and never needs to be restated too often.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul describes his apostolic ministry in priestly terms: he is a leitourgos (liturgical minister) offering the Gentile nations as a sacrifice pleasing to God. The cultic language is striking — the missionary's work is priestly work, the Gentiles themselves are the offering, and the Holy Spirit is what makes the offering acceptable. The pride Paul expresses is not personal vanity but the legitimate joy of a craftsman whose work has been effective — 'in Christ Jesus,' grounding the boast entirely in the one through whom the work was done.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's missionary report: from Jerusalem (where the church began) to Illyricum (modern Croatia — the western edge of the Balkans) — a geographic arc spanning the entire eastern Mediterranean. The method was comprehensive: word (preaching), deed (acts of mercy and service), signs and wonders (authenticating miracles), and the power of the Spirit. The subject of all of it is Christ: 'what Christ has accomplished through me.' Paul is not the protagonist of his own missionary report; he is the instrument through whom Christ has been building his church.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's ambition is one of the most focused and principled statements of missionary strategy in Scripture: go where Christ has not yet been named. Not because the churches that already exist need no support, but because his specific gift and calling is pioneer evangelism — breaking new ground, planting the gospel in virgin soil, leaving behind a church that will then do what it takes to reach its own region.

The citation of Isaiah 52:15 — originally about the Servant's impact on the nations who had not heard of him — is applied to Paul's own mission: he is the one through whom the Isaiah prophecy is being fulfilled, as the gospel goes to those who have never heard. Every faithful missionary sent to unreached peoples is doing what Paul did and fulfilling what Isaiah foresaw.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's long-deferred visit is not indifference — it is the discipline of a pioneer missionary who will not plant where others have already sowed (v. 20). The eastern Mediterranean has been evangelized; his work there is done. Rome is now within reach not as a destination but as a staging post for the westward advance. The 'longing for many years' is the longing of a missionary held back from his next frontier by the unfinished work at the current one.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Helped on my journey' (propemphthēnai) — a technical term for missionary support: financial provision, prayer, perhaps letters of introduction. Paul is not merely passing through Rome; he is asking for partnership in the Spanish mission. This is the practical purpose behind the most theological letter ever written: Romans is a theological masterpiece and a church-planting strategy document, the long-form theological introduction of a missionary seeking a new base of operations.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalem collection — Paul's great ecumenical project — represents the material unity of the church expressed across its geographic and ethnic divisions. The Macedonian and Achaian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth) have contributed from their own poverty and prosperity respectively. This gift is both humanitarian relief for the materially poor Jerusalem church and a theological statement: the Gentile churches acknowledge their debt to the Jewish root from which they have grown.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be in material things to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They owe it to them' — the debt is real and its direction is clear: the Gentiles received the gospel through Israel, the Scriptures from Israel, the Messiah out of Israel. Material support for the Jewish poor is the Gentile church's tangible acknowledgment of this incalculable spiritual indebtedness. The collection is not charity in the patronizing sense — it is the payment of a debt freely and joyfully acknowledged by those who know how much they have received.

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The fullness of the blessing of Christ' — Paul anticipates his visit to Rome not as a tourist or a theological celebrity but as an apostle carrying the full weight of Christ's saving grace. The phrase is dense with confidence: not his own blessing, not the church's blessing, but Christ's — the comprehensive riches of the gospel made available through apostolic ministry. Whatever Jerusalem brings (acceptance or rejection of the collection, imprisonment or release), the blessing Paul will bring to Rome is secured not by his circumstances but by the Christ he serves.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Strive together with me in your prayers' — the word is synagōnizomai: to agonize alongside, the language of athletic contest. Paul is asking for the serious, costly, sustained prayer that matches the stakes of what he is about to do. He fears two things: violence from unbelievers in Judea (his Jewish opponents who had dogged his ministry) and rejection from the Jerusalem church (who may refuse the Gentile collection). Both fears proved justified; but prayer is the weapon he commends for both dangers.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By God's will' — Paul holds even his own travel plans with open hands. He wants joy, refreshment, the company of the Roman church — but he submits all of it to the will of God. The closing benediction ('the God of peace be with you all') echoes the opening ('grace and peace' — 1:7) and the prayer of 15:5 ('the God of endurance and encouragement'). The God of peace — who made peace through the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20) and whose peace passes understanding (Philippians 4:7) — is the one Paul commends to the church he has not yet met but already loves.

16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Romans 16 is sometimes treated as an appendix — a list of greetings to be skimmed before putting the letter down. It is far more than that. The thirty-five individuals and households Paul greets by name constitute a remarkable social portrait of the early Roman church: women who laboured hard in the Lord, a former slave, co-workers who risked their necks for Paul, a member of Caesar's household. The community Paul is writing to and for is not an abstraction; it is these people, in this city, with these names and these stories.

The chapter also contains a sharp warning against those who create division and cause obstacles contrary to the doctrine (vv. 17–20) — a reminder that the unity and the gospel Paul has laboured to establish require vigilance as well as love. And then the letter ends where it began: with the gospel. The doxology of vv. 25–27 is one of the most comprehensive summaries of Paul's gospel in the New Testament — the mystery kept secret for long ages, now disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The list of greetings in Romans 16 is the most extensive in Paul's letters and has been called "a window into the earliest church" by scholars of early Christianity. Twenty-six individuals are named, along with several households and groups. The social diversity is remarkable: Phoebe, a deacon and patron from Cenchreae; Priscilla and Aquila, tentmakers and theological teachers; Andronicus and Junia, "outstanding among the apostles" and Christians before Paul; Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia; Mary, who worked very hard. Slaves and free, women and men, Jews and Gentiles — all members of the same body.

Phoebe (vv. 1–2) deserves special notice: Paul commends her as a deacon (diakonos — the same word used of male church officers) of the church in Cenchreae, and as a patron (prostatis) who has been of help to many, including Paul himself. She was almost certainly the letter-carrier — the person who bore the manuscript of Romans from Corinth to Rome and, as was customary for letter-carriers in antiquity, would have read and explained the letter to its recipients. The greatest theological letter ever written was entrusted to a woman for its first public delivery.

The greeting "holy kiss" (v. 16) — appearing in all of Paul's letters — was the physical expression of the family bond that the gospel created. In the ancient world, the kiss of greeting was reserved for family members. The church that greeted one another with a holy kiss was declaring, physically and publicly, that these people — strangers by blood, foreigners by origin, divided by every social category — were family. The gospel had done what nothing else could do: created a new human community that crossed every boundary the ancient world had erected.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Humanity

Romans 16:1–16 is the embodiment in flesh-and-blood names of Paul's theological argument in chapters 1–15. The "no distinction between Jew and Greek" of 10:12, the olive tree of Jew and Gentile grafted together of 11:17–24, the "welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you" of 15:7 — all of these are visible in the list of names. This is what the gospel looks like when it has done its work: Phoebe and Priscilla and Andronicus and Junia, the patron and the tentmaker, the first convert and the former persecutor's associates, all belonging to each other in Christ. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a sociology.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The social mixing of Romans 16 was, by the standards of the first-century world, radical to the point of scandalous. Social boundaries in Rome were enforced with rigour; meals with social inferiors were a form of self-humiliation. The church that gathered Phoebe and the member of Caesar's household and the freed slave and the Jewish tentmakers for common worship and common greeting was an institution the Roman world had no category for. Now: The contemporary church's ability or inability to embody the social diversity of Romans 16 is one of the most important tests of its gospel fidelity. A church that is racially, socially, or economically homogeneous by design has stopped short of what the gospel creates. The greetings of Romans 16 are not an antiquarian curiosity; they are the template for the new humanity the gospel is building.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's commendation of Phoebe is the introduction of the letter's bearer to its recipients. She is a deacon of the church — a recognised officer in Christian service — and a patron who has used her financial resources and social standing to support Paul and others in their ministry. The combination is significant: she is both a servant of the church and a leader within it, both one who has received the gospel and one who has enabled its advance.

The instruction to welcome her "in a way worthy of the saints" and to "help her in whatever she may need" is the hospitality principle of the ancient church made concrete. Phoebe is coming to a city where she may know no one; the Roman church is being instructed to treat her as one of their own — which, in Christ, she is.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary: Prisca (Priscilla) and Aquila — the tent-making couple who had sheltered Paul in Corinth (Acts 18) and taught Apollos more accurately (Acts 18:26) — are at the top of the list. 'Risked their necks' is almost certainly literal: at some point they placed themselves in mortal danger to protect Paul's life. The gratitude of all the Gentile churches is owed to them — their courage at a particular moment may have preserved the ministry that evangelized the western Mediterranean. The personal names in Romans 16 are a reminder that the gospel moves through specific, costly, named human lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The church in their house' — the early church met in homes; there were no purpose-built church buildings for centuries. Prisca and Aquila's home was the gathering place for one of Rome's house churches, a pattern they had practiced in Corinth and Ephesus as well. Epaenetus, the 'first convert in Asia' — the firstfruits of Paul's Ephesian ministry, now living in Rome. His presence there is a reminder that the gospel traveled through the empire by moving people, not just ideas: converted in Ephesus, now carrying the faith to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners, who are well known to the apostles, and who also were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Mary 'worked hard' — the verb (kopiaō) is the same word Paul uses for his own apostolic labor. Junia (most likely a woman, the feminine form of the name) is greeted with Andronicus as 'well known to the apostles' — notable among those who bore authoritative witness to the resurrection. Both are described as Paul's 'kinsmen' (fellow Jews) and 'fellow prisoners' — they had shared imprisonment with him, a bond forged in suffering. 'In Christ before me' — they were converts before Paul's Damascus road encounter, part of the earliest Jerusalem community.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary: Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys — common names in Roman slave households, suggesting that the early Roman church included significant numbers from the lower social strata. 'My beloved in the Lord' is Paul's warmest personal designation: not merely acquaintances or ministry colleagues but those for whom he holds genuine affection rooted in the common life they share in Christ. The church Paul greets is a community of the beloved, held together not by social class or ethnic origin but by their shared belovedness in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Approved in Christ' (dokimos) — the language of testing and verification. Apelles has been tried and found genuine, his faith tested and proved. The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus (likely prominent Roman households whose members had become believers) are greeted as communities within the larger community: the church existed in pockets within Roman society, gathering across the household lines that organized that society. Herodion, another Jewish kinsman, is singled out for personal mention.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three women workers in the Lord: Tryphaena and Tryphosa (whose names mean 'dainty' and 'delicate' — perhaps twins, perhaps ironic given their hard labor) and Persis, who 'worked hard in the Lord.' Women are prominent among Paul's named co-workers throughout his letters, a pattern that reflects the genuine inclusion of women in the mission of the early church. Rufus (possibly the son of Simon of Cyrene, Mark 15:21) is 'chosen in the Lord' — a mark of particular divine regard; his mother's care for Paul is remembered with filial gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two more clusters of house-church communities, each with their circle of unnamed saints. The names span the social spectrum: some are common slave names (Hermes, Hermas), others appear in Roman aristocratic records. The church in Rome was genuinely cross-social — slave and free, men and women, Jews and Gentiles gathered around the one name. 'The saints who are with them' reminds us that for every named believer in the New Testament, there were hundreds of unnamed ones whose faithfulness built the church that reached us.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The holy kiss — practiced across the early church as the physical sign of the family bond that the gospel creates — crosses every social barrier that the ancient world erected. Slave and free, Jew and Gentile, male and female greet one another with the same gesture that family members exchange. 'All the churches of Christ greet you' — Paul bears the solidarity of the entire Gentile mission to the Roman church: they are not alone, not isolated, but part of a community spanning the Mediterranean world, united by the name of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before the closing doxology, Paul inserts a sharp warning (vv. 17–20) against those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine the Romans have been taught. The letter has been, among other things, a sustained argument for the unity of the body across the strong/weak divide; it would be a bitter irony if the letter itself became a tool of division. Paul's instruction is clear: watch them, avoid them. The divisive person — whatever their theological credentials — is not serving Christ but their own appetites, and they deceive the naive with smooth talk and flattery.

The closing doxology (vv. 25–27) returns to the letter's great themes for one final, comprehensive statement. God is able to strengthen — the power of the gospel is not an argument but a strengthening. According to Paul's gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ — these are identified: Paul's gospel is the gospel of Jesus Christ, not a human theological construct. According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages — the gospel is not a new invention; it is the disclosure of what God planned from before time began. Now made known to all the nations — the universality Paul has argued throughout. For the obedience of faith — the phrase that bracketed the letter in 1:5 now closes it. To the only wise God — the doxology of chapter 11 returns, now applied to the whole letter's argument. Through Jesus Christ — the mediator of all grace and all glory. To whom be glory forever. Amen.

The letter that began with Paul introducing himself as a slave of Christ and set apart for the gospel ends with everything returning to God — from him, through him, and to him. The argument is complete. The doxology is the only adequate conclusion. Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Revealed: Gospel and Old Testament Unity

Romans 16:25–27 returns to the theme announced in 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets; the Old Testament is the gospel in anticipation; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. The "mystery" kept secret for long ages is not something the Old Testament was ignorant of but something it was pregnant with — the inclusion of the Gentiles in the covenant people, the extension of the Abrahamic blessing to all nations, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. Calvin's canon of interpretation applies: the two testaments are one Bible, one gospel, one covenant of grace, administered differently but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning of vv. 17–20 against divisive teachers was written into the most doctrinally comprehensive letter Paul ever wrote. The letter's very depth makes it susceptible to misuse: its teachings on election, freedom, and grace can all be distorted into weapons of division. Paul's warning is therefore structurally appropriate — the deeper the theology, the greater the need for vigilance against those who weaponise it. Now: Every generation produces its version of the smooth-talking divisive teacher who uses theological language to advance personal agendas and create factions. Paul's three-fold response is the standing instruction: watch them carefully; avoid them; trust the God of peace who will soon crush Satan under your feet (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. — Romans 16:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
The command is pointed and practical: watch and avoid. The divisive teacher is not to be engaged endlessly in debate or accommodated indefinitely in the hope that he will improve. He is to be identified and avoided — not with contempt, but with the clear-sightedness of people who know what they have been taught and can recognise a deviation when they see it.

"Contrary to the doctrine you have been taught" — the standard of judgment is not novelty versus tradition, or majority versus minority opinion. It is the apostolic teaching — the gospel Paul has spent sixteen chapters expounding. The community that has this letter has the measuring rod. Apply it. And where teaching measures short or crooked, act accordingly.

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wise as to what is good, innocent as to what is evil' — the positive and negative of the same counsel. In a world of sophisticated evil and manipulation, the Christian is to be genuinely knowledgeable about goodness (not naive) and genuinely innocent of evil (not sophisticated in wickedness). 'The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet' — an echo of Genesis 3:15 (the first gospel promise: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head), now applied to the whole community through their union with Christ who has already won the decisive victory.

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: Timothy, Paul's closest colleague throughout the Gentile mission, sends greetings — a sign of the collegial nature of Paul's apostolic work. The three Jewish co-workers (his 'kinsmen') represent the Jewish component of what has been a predominantly Gentile mission. And then Tertius breaks through: the amanuensis who wrote the letter inserts his own greeting. He is not merely a scribe — he is a brother in Christ, himself part of the community to which the letter is addressed, a co-laborer in the work of preserving and transmitting Paul's apostolic word.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Gaius (likely the Corinthian Gaius of 1 Corinthians 1:14, baptized by Paul) hosted Paul and hosted the whole church — a man of sufficient means and sufficient generosity to open his home as the gathering place for the entire Corinthian community. Erastus the 'city treasurer' (oikonomos) is remarkable: an inscription found at Corinth reads 'Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid the pavement at his own expense.' A senior municipal official belonging to the Roman church — evidence that the gospel had penetrated even the highest levels of Corinthian civic life.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: A second benediction of grace — the word that opened the letter (1:5, 1:7) closes it. From first to last, Romans is a letter about grace: the grace of apostleship (1:5), the grace of justification (3:24), the grace of election (11:5), the grace of spiritual gifts (12:6), and now the closing grace of the Lord Jesus Christ commended to the whole community. Nothing is more fitting as the final word of the greatest letter ever written about the gospel than the name and grace of the one the gospel is about.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary: The doxology that closes Romans is addressed to God 'who is able to strengthen you' — and the means of that strengthening is 'my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ.' The gospel is not merely information about Christ; it is the power by which God strengthens his people (cf. 1:16). The 'mystery kept secret for long ages but now disclosed' is the inclusion of the Gentiles in the one people of God through the Messiah — the great open secret that the prophets pointed toward and that Paul has been expounding throughout the letter. The command of the eternal God drives the Gentile mission.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The only wise God' — not one wise being among many, but the only one whose wisdom is absolute, uncreated, inexhaustible, and without rival. All of Romans has been a display of divine wisdom: the wisdom that designed salvation through the cross, that included the Gentiles through Israel's stumbling, that will bring Israel in through the Gentiles' fullness, that will sum up all things in Christ. 'Be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ' — all glory returns to God through the mediation of the Son, who is both the agent of creation and the mediator of new creation. Amen: so it is, and so it shall be, world without end.
